rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds.

Change temperature alone to probe selectivity in the tightly clustered middle peaks and the final pair. The broad gradient preserves reliable elution while revealing whether heating improves the critical separations.

Probe the opposite temperature limit with the same gradient to map selectivity changes and possible elution-order reversals. This will identify the most promising temperature region before adjusting gradient slope.

Keep the favorable low-temperature selectivity and reduce the gradient slope to improve the two unresolved pairs. The current 6.34-minute elution endpoint leaves room to gain resolution while targeting a last peak below 10 minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction while keeping the gradient duration fixed, giving a shallower slope without extending the elution window. This should test whether the remaining critical pair can reach baseline resolution before 10 minutes.

Use a shallower gradient than injection 4 with a modestly higher starting organic fraction to offset the added retention time. This targets improved separation of the remaining critical pair while keeping the final peak near or below 10 minutes.

Injection 6 achieved the maximum CRF; now raise the starting organic fraction one step to seek a shorter fully resolved separation. Keep temperature and duration unchanged to test whether its resolution margin survives the earlier elution.

Lower the final organic fraction one step to slightly reduce the gradient slope and recover the small resolution deficit in injection 7. This should preserve much of its time advantage over injection 6 while targeting full resolution.

Raise temperature one step from the faster fully resolved method to test whether retention can be shortened without losing baseline separation. Injection 8 provides some resolution margin, but temperature-dependent selectivity must be checked directly.

Return to 25 C and narrow the gradient window: the higher starting fraction should shorten retention, while the lower slope may preserve the critical separation. This tests a faster alternative to the fully resolved 9.18-minute result.

Slightly flatten the gradient to improve the critical middle separation, and use 30 C to offset the added retention. The larger preceding gap in injection 10 may accommodate the temperature-driven selectivity shift that limited injection 9.

Lower temperature one step to restore separation of the final pair while retaining the shallower gradient needed for the middle pair. This may deliver full resolution slightly faster than injection 8.

Test whether a larger temperature increase moves the near-coeluting pairs past their selectivity crossings into a faster, resolved elution pattern. Injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method if this higher-temperature branch fails.

Continue the temperature-selectivity scan at the same shallow gradient to see whether the middle cluster separates after further elution-order changes. A resolved method in this region could substantially shorten the current 8.99-minute endpoint.

Check the upper temperature limit with the shallow gradient, since the unresolved pairs at 50 C may separate after selectivity crossings. This completes the broad temperature scan while retaining injection 12 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test a faster-gradient branch: the middle pair reversed order between injections 3 and 4, suggesting that a steeper gradient may also separate it. Use 30 C to improve the late-pair separation that limited the original fast, low-temperature run.

Moderately flatten the fast gradient to open the compressed middle cluster, while raising the starting organic fraction to limit retention and alter selectivity. This tests whether the short-run branch can achieve full resolution rather than returning immediately to the nine-minute method.

Raise the starting fraction and moderately reduce the slope to expand the short-run middle cluster without greatly extending retention. This probes whether starting-composition selectivity can recover both deficient pairs from injection 17.

Injection 18 is nearly fully resolved; raise the starting fraction and flatten the gradient together to target both small resolution deficits. The higher start should offset the longer gradient and preserve a short elution window.

Lower temperature one step to open the remaining middle-cluster gap in injection 19. Its other separations have useful margin, so this may achieve full resolution with only a modest increase from the 3.96-minute endpoint.

Shorten the gradient by one step from the new fastest fully resolved method. Injection 20 has resolution margin in every pair, so this tests a shorter endpoint while keeping its favorable starting composition and temperature.
Test a higher starting organic fraction for earlier elution, paired with a shallower slope to protect the sensitive middle pair. Injection 21 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Return to the best starting composition and test a modestly steeper gradient with a shorter programmed duration. This probes the speed limit near injection 21, whose critical pair was just above baseline resolution.

Lower the starting organic fraction one step to improve the middle-cluster gap, while using a steeper gradient to offset the added retention. This tests a neighboring fast-method branch; injection 21 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved option.

Shorten the programmed gradient while preserving injection 21’s slope and composition trajectory throughout its observed elution window. The gradient ends at the outlet at 4.65 minutes, after its 4.14-minute last peak, so this should retain full resolution and the maximum CRF.
